claims.label: Theorem 3.3
claims.statement_original: For any family of scores $(S_{k+1},\dots,S_{n+m})$ satisfying Assumptions 2 and 3, the empirical $p$-values defined in (10) are PRDS on ${\mathcal{H}}_0$ and the null $p$-values are super-uniform. In particular, under Assumptions 1 and 3, this result holds for the $p$-values generated by AdaDetect with a score function satisfying (8).

claims.label: Theorem 3.4
claims.statement_original:
Consider any family of scores $(S_{k+1},\dots,S_{n+m})$ satisfying Assumptions 2 and 3. Let $R_\alpha$ denote the rejection set of BH procedure applied to $p$-values defined in (10) at level $\alpha$. Then, for any distribution $P\in \mathcal{P}$, 
\[
\mathrm{FDR}(P,R_\alpha)=  \sum_{i\in {\mathcal{H}}_0}  \mathbb{E}\left(\frac{ \lfloor \alpha (\ell+1)K_i/m\rfloor }{(\ell +1) K_i}\right),\tag{11}
\]
 where $K_i$ is a random variable that takes values in $\{1,\dots,m\}$ for any $i \in {\mathcal{H}}_0$. In particular, under Assumptions 1 and 3, (11) holds with $R_\alpha=\mbox{AdaDetect}_{\alpha}$, the AdaDetect procedure at level $\alpha$.

claims.label: Theorem 3.6
claims.statement_original:
In the setting of Theorem 3.4, denote $p=(p_i,1\leq i\leq m)$ the family of empirical $p$-values defined in (10) and consider any function $G : [0,1]^m \rightarrow (0,\infty)$ that is coordinate-wise nondecreasing. Then the procedure, denoted by $R_{\alpha m/G(p)}$, combining the BH algorithm at level $\alpha m/G(p)$ with these empirical $p$-values is such that, for any parameter $P\in \mathcal{P}$, 
\[
\mathrm{FDR}(P,R_{\alpha m/G(p) }) \leq  \alpha \sum_{i\in {\mathcal{H}}_0}  \mathbb{E}_{p'\sim \mathcal{D}_i}\left(\frac{1}{G(p')} \right),\tag{14}
\]
 where $\mathcal{D}_{i}$ is defined by (13). In particular, this FDR expression holds for $R_{\alpha m/G(p) }=\mbox{AdaDetect}_{{\alpha m/G(p) }}$ under Assumptions 1 and 3.

claims.label: Theorem 4.1
claims.statement_original: Assume Assumptions 4 and 5 hold. The likelihood ratio function $r(\cdot)$ defined in (18) is an optimal score function in the sense that the rejection set $R=\{i \in \{1,\dots,m\}\::\: r(X_i)\geq c(\alpha)\}$, where $c(\alpha)\in (0,1)$ is chosen such that $\mbox{mFDR}(R)=\alpha$ (assuming it exists), has a higher TPR than any rejection set $R'=\{i \in \{1,\dots,m\}\::\: r'(X_i)\geq c'\}$ where $c'\in \mathbb{R}$ and $r':\mathcal{Z}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ is measurable with mFDR at most $\alpha$.

claims.label: Theorem 5.1
claims.statement_original:
Consider the setting of Theorem 4.1. Assume $\alpha, \beta\in (0,1)$, $k,m_1\geq 1$, and $g^\sharp_\mathcal{G}$, defined in (27), satisfies $R_0(g^\sharp_\mathcal{G}) = \beta$. Fix any $\delta\in (0,1/2)$. Then there exist constants $C,C'>0$ that only depend on $\delta$ such that, if 
\[
\epsilon_0 = C\sqrt{\frac{V(\mathcal{G}) + \log(1/\delta)}{k}}, \quad \Delta = C' \gamma^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{V(\mathcal{G}) + \log(1/\delta)}{k\wedge \ell}},\tag{28}
\]
 where $\gamma$ is defined in (17), the following results hold.

(i) With probability at least $1-\delta$, ${R}_0(\hat{g})  \leq \beta + \Delta$ and ${R}_1(\hat{g}) \leq {R}_1(g^\sharp_\mathcal{G}) + \Delta.$

(ii) Let $M = \lceil (1-{R}_1(g^\sharp_\mathcal{G})-\Delta) m_1\rceil$. Assume that 
\[
1-{R}_1(g^\sharp_\mathcal{G})  \geq  (1+\alpha^{-1})  \Delta, \quad \ell\geq \frac{2 m}{\alpha M}, \quad \beta \le \frac{0.4\alpha M}{m}. \tag{29}
\]
 Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$, 
\[
\mbox{AdaDetect}_\alpha \supset \{i\in \{1,\dots,m\}\::\: \hat{g}(X_i)\geq 0\},\tag{30}
\]



\[
|\mbox{AdaDetect}_\alpha\cap {\mathcal{H}}_1|/m_1\geq 1-{R}_1(g^\sharp_\mathcal{G})-\Delta,\tag{31}
\]
 where $\mbox{AdaDetect}_\alpha$ denotes the rejection set of AdaDetect with score function $\hat{g}$.

claims.label: Theorem 5.4
claims.statement_original:
Fix any $r\in \{0,\dots,m\}$ and let $\mathcal{R}=\{|\mbox{AdaDetect}^*_\alpha|\geq r\}$. Assume $m\geq 1$, $\ell, k\geq 0$, $n=k+\ell\geq 1$, and $\overline{G}_0$ (33) is continuous and strictly decreasing. Under Assumptions 4 and 5, for any $\delta,\eta\in (0,1)$ such that $(\ell+1)\delta\alpha(r\vee 1)/m\geq 2$, 
\[
\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{R} \cap\{\mbox{AdaDetect}^*_\alpha\subset \mbox{AdaDetect}_{\alpha'}\}^c\right)\leq \mathbb{P}\left(\hat{\eta}> \eta \right) + 2 m e^{-(3/28)  (\ell+1)\delta^2\alpha(r\vee 1)/m},\tag{36}
\]
 where $\alpha'=\alpha(1+3\delta)(1+\zeta_r(\eta))$ and $\zeta_r(\cdot)$ and $\hat{\eta}$ are defined in (34) and (35), respectively. Furthermore, (36) is also true with $\mbox{AdaDetect}^*_\alpha$ replaced by $\mathrm{BH}^*_\alpha$, the BH algorithm applied to the oracle $p$-values $p^*_i=\overline{G}_0(g^*(X_i))$, $1\leq i\leq m$.

members.local_label: Section 2.1 — null training sample, test sample and model
members.source_heading: Section 2.1 — null training sample, test sample and model
members.statement_original: As in Section 1.1, we let $Y = (Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$ denote the null training sample (NTS) with a common marginal distribution $P_0$, $X = (X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ the test sample with $X_i\sim P_i$ ($1\leq i\leq m$), $Z = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_{n+m}) =(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n, X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ the full sample, ${\mathcal{H}}_0=\{1\leq i\leq m\::\: P_i = P_0\}$ the set of nulls in the test sample with $m_0 = |{\mathcal{H}}_0|, \pi_0 = m_0 / m$, and ${\mathcal{H}}_1=\{1,\dots,m\}\setminus {\mathcal{H}}_0$ the set of novelties with $m_1 = |{\mathcal{H}}_1|, \pi_1 = m_1 / m$. For notational convenience, we write $n+{\mathcal{H}}_0$ for the set $\{n+i,i\in {\mathcal{H}}_0\}$. Furthermore, we denote by $P$ the joint distribution of $Z$, which belongs to a family of distributions $\mathcal{P}$ (model).

members.statement_original:
Suppose a set of $p$-values $(p_i,1\leq i\leq m)$ is available, the BH algorithm Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) returns $R = \{i\in \{1,\dots,m\}\::\:p_i\leq \alpha \hat{k}/m\},$ where $\alpha$ is the target FDR level and

\hat{k} = \max\left\{k\in \{0,\dots,m\}\::\: \sum_{i=1}^m {\mathbb{1}\left\{p_i\leq \alpha k/m\right\}}\geq k\right\}.\tag{4}
\]

members.statement_original:
In this paper, we propose a method called AdaDetect. It is an adaptive novelty detection procedure that extends the existing strategies described in Weinstein et al. (2017), Yang et al. (2021), Mary and Roquain (2022), and Bates et al. (2021). It starts by splitting the null sample $(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)$ in two samples $(Y_1,\dots,Y_k)$ and $(Y_{k+1},\dots,Y_{n})$ with $k\geq 0$. To avoid cluttering our notation, we define $\ell$ as the size of the second null sample, i.e., $\ell=n - k.$ It proceeds with the following steps.

1.  Compute a data-driven score function of form 
\[
g(z)=g(z,(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{k}), (Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n +m})),\:\:\: z\in \mathcal{Z},\tag{7}
\]
 which satisfies the following invariance property: for any permutation $\pi$ of $\{k+1,\dots,n+m\}$ and $z,z_1,\dots,z_{n+m}\in \mathcal{Z}$, we have 
\[
g(z,(z_{1},\dots,z_{k}), (z_{\pi(k+1)},\dots,z_{\pi(n +m)}))=g(z,(z_{1},\dots,z_{k}), (z_{k+1},\dots,z_{n +m})).\tag{8}
\]


2.  Transform the raw data into univariate scores 
\[
S_i = g(Z_i; (Z_1,\dots,Z_k) , (Z_{k+1},\dots,Z_{n+m})), \quad i \in \{ k+1, \ldots,n+m\}.\tag{9}
\]
 Here, we assume that novelties typically have large scores.

3.  For each test point $X_j$, generate the empirical $p$-value by comparing $S_i$ with the scores in the NTS: 
\[
p_j = \frac{1}{\ell+1}\left(1+\sum_{i=k+1}^{n}{\mathbb{1}\left\{S_i>S_{n+j}\right\}}\right), \:\:j\in\{1,\dots,m\}.\tag{10}
\]


4.  Apply the BH algorithm to $(p_1,\dots,p_m)$ at the target level $\alpha$.

We will call this procedure $\mbox{AdaDetect}_\alpha$ in the sequel to emphasize the target level.

members.statement_original:

members.source_heading: Section 2.2 — false discovery rate and false discovery proportion, equation (2)
members.statement_original:
Given a procedure $R$, the false discovery rate (FDR) is defined as the expectation of the false discovery proportion (FDP) with respect to the distribution $P\in \mathcal{P}$: 
\[
\mathrm{FDR}(P,R)= \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P}[\mathrm{FDP}(P,R)],\:\:\: \mathrm{FDP}(P,R)=\frac{\sum_{i\in {\mathcal{H}}_0} {\mathbb{1}\left\{i\in R\right\}}}{1\vee |R|}.\tag{2}
\]

members.statement_original: Recall that AdaDetect is equivalent to applying the counting knockoff on the scores which relies on an estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}$ (Section 2.4). For each given $t$, when $\ell$ and $m$ is large, $\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}(t)\approx m \:\mathbb{P}_{S_i\sim P_0}(S_i \ge t)/\mathbb{E}[|R(t)|] \approx \mathbb{E}[|R(t)\cap \{k+1, \ldots, n\}|]/\mathbb{E}[|R(t)|],$ where $R(t)$ is set of rejections at threshold $t$. The RHS is called the marginal FDR (mFDR), an error metric that is close to FDR when $|R(t)|$ is large and often used for asymptotic power analysis of FDR-controlling procedures e.g. Sun and Cai (2007); Lei and Fithian (2018). The following theorem derives the optimal score function among all procedures that reject hypotheses with $S_i$ above some thresholds subject to mFDR control (see Weinstein (2021); Rosset et al. (2022) for results for FDR instead of mFDR).

interfaces.name: PRDS
interfaces.type_shape: For each null index and increasing measurable set, its conditional probability given that p-value equals u is nondecreasing in u; include the increasing-set footnote.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: For each null index and increasing measurable set, its conditional probability given that p-value equals u is nondecreasing in u; include the increasing-set footnote. Original source domains and conventions are preserved; this is not a library audit.

members.statement_original:
Following Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001), we say a family of $p$-values $(p_i,1\leq i\leq m)$ is PRDS on ${\mathcal{H}}_0$ if, for any $i\in {\mathcal{H}}_0$ and nondecreasing[^1] measurable set $D\subset [0,1]^m$, the function $u\in [0,1]\mapsto \mathbb{P}((p_j,1\leq j\leq m)\in D\:|\: p_i= u)$ is nondecreasing.

[^1]: A set $D\subset [0,1]^m$ is said to be nondecreasing if for any $x\in D$ and $y\in [0,1]^m$, we have $y\in D$ provided that $y_i\geq x_i$ for all $i$.

members.statement_original:
Since AdaDetect is invariant under any strictly monotone transformation of the score function (see Remark 2.1), AdaDetect$^*$ can be realized as any AdaDetect procedure with a score function of the form 
\[
g^*= \Psi \circ r, \mbox{ for some increasing continuous $\Psi:(0,1)\to {\mathbb{R}}$},\tag{19}
\]
 where $\Psi$ could depend on unknown parameters. This is a crucial property of AdaDetect that enables flexible classification methods to construct score functions without concerning about the composition of nulls and novelties that may change the oracle score $r$.
